maddeler.e: الْأُرْدُن or الْأُرْدُنّ • (al-ʔurdun or al-ʔurdunn) m
maddeler.t:
Etymology tree
Proto-Semitic *warad-?
Biblical Hebrew יַרְדֵּן (yardēn)der.
Aramaicbor.
Arabic الأردن
From جُنْد الْأُرْدُنّ (jund al-ʔurdunn), “the military district of Jordan”, probably directly borrowed from the Aramaic isolect spoken there at the time, attested by the written Jewish Babylonian Aramaic and Jewish Literary Aramaic as יֹורְדְּנא (yordənā) and יַרְדְּנא (yardənā). Both forms give the present Arabic one regularly: The emphatic state ending was rendered by the Arabic article, and the distinction of the onset consonants /j/, /ʔ/ and /ʕ/ either had already little functional load, in the same fashion as the etyma of هُود (hūd), يَافُوخ (yāfūḵ), يَلَب (yalab), الْعِرَاق (al-ʕirāq) etc., or the onset يُـ (yu-) or the pattern of *يَرْدُن (*yardun) or *أَرْدُن (*ʔardun) in Arabic was hardly admissible and had to be regularized, that is classicized. See Hebrew יַרְדֵּן (yardén) for the ultimate derivation of the toponym.
g: Jordan (a country in West Asia in the Middle East)
Jordan (a river in West Asia in the Middle East, that empties into the Dead Sea, flowing through Israel, the Golan Heights, the West Bank and Jordan)

maddeler.e: انا • (ʔanā) m or f
الْعِرَاق • (al-ʕirāq) f
maddeler.t:
In medieval Arabic geography, the toponym referred to the southern and central parts of present-day Iraq. The word was taken as the definite form of عِرَاق (ʕirāq, “shore, edge, any land next to water”), in contrast with الْجَزِيرَة (al-jazīra, “the Arabian Peninsula”), called ܓܙܺܝܪܬܴ݁ܐ (gəzīrtā, “Mesopotamia”) in Syriac.
Some sources suggest an origin in Middle Persian. Forms like [script needed] (ˀyrg /⁠ērag⁠/) or [script needed] (ˀl'k' /⁠erāg⁠/, “lowlands”) are related to the same root as 𐭠𐭩𐭥𐭠𐭭 (ʾyrʾn /⁠ērān⁠/, “Iran”) and 𐭠𐭩𐭫 (ʾyl /⁠ēr⁠/, “Iranian”), reflecting the influence of Persia, Iraq’s plateau neighbor. The form [script needed] (ērag) is also found in a Jewish Babylonian Aramaic incantation bowl, which preserves the oldest known written form of “Iraq” as אירג (ʔyrg /⁠*ērag⁠/, “Iraq”).
The Aramaic continuum may have preserved a pharyngealized variant, comparable to rare forms such as عِرْنَاس (ʕirnās, “distaff”) and عَمْرُوسَة (ʕamrūsa, “small lamb”).
A connection with Akkadian 𒌷𒀕 (/⁠uruk⁠/, “Uruk”) is unlikely on phonetic grounds.

From the Nabataean Aramaic letter 𐢁 (l, “aleph”), derived from the Phoenician letter 𐤀 (l, “ālef”), from the Egyptian hieroglyph 𓃾. See also Classical Syriac ܐ (l, “ālef”), Hebrew א (l, “alef”), Ancient Greek Α (A), Latin A.
g: Although usually considered to be the first letter of the Arabic alphabet, the small hamza (ء (ʔ)) that sits on top of أ (ʔ) is really the first letter of the Arabic alphabet, and the tall column is its bearer, together known as alif mahmūza (أَلِف مهموزة, hamzated alif). This entry only deals with the lower part, the bearer, which is called أَلِف (ʔalif) and, without the hamza, is used to lengthen a preceding a.

maddeler.e: اللَّات • (al-lāt) f
maddeler.t:
Uncertain. Possible etymologies:
* From the root ل ت ت (l t t), from which the verb لَتَّ (latta, “to mix, or knead, barley-meal”) is derived. This is the explanation given in Arab lexicographical tradition and supported by epigraphic evidence; compare Hismaic 𐪁𐪉 (lt).
* A feminine form of اللّٰه (allāh) or الإلٰه (al-ʔilāh). This is supported by the form given by Herodotus, who identifies Ἀλιλᾱ́τ (Alilā́t) (which would correspond to *اَلْإِلَات (*alʔilāt)) with Aphrodite Urania, and is explained as having the same ending as some ossified vocative forms like أَخَات (ʔaḵāt) for أُخْت (ʔuḵt, “sister”). However, many gods and goddesses were referred to by the titles الإلٰه (al-ʔilāh) and الإِلٰهَة (al-ʔilāha), and so it is not certain that the goddess referenced by Herodotus is the same.

maddeler.e: الرُّوح الْقُدُس • (ar-rūḥ al-qudus) m
maddeler.t: Translation of Ancient Greek ἅγιον (hágion, “holy”) πνεῦμα (pneûma, “spirit”). First attested in Arabic in the Quran at 2:253, in the form of روح القدس (rūḥu l-qudusi), that is as a proper genitive construction.
g: The Holy Spirit (one of God’s three eternal natures)

maddeler.e: الزُّهَرَة • (az-zuhara) f
maddeler.t: Related to زُهْرَة (zuhra, “brilliance, brightness, radiance, beauty”); Venus is the brightest object in the night sky (after the moon).

maddeler.e: الْمُشْتَرِي • (al-muštarī) m
maddeler.t:
* From مُشْتَرٍ (muštarin, “buyer, seller”), from the root ش ر ي (š r y) with the original semantic sense of bringing of goods or commodities (to be exchanged). This renders the title to mean "the bringer of goods", "provider of commodities", or "supplier of fortunes"; parallel with the planet's other names also denoting fortune and its auspicious nature.
* Alternatively from the root ش ر ي (š r y) in the sense of "being persistent", "to be reliable"; possibly parallel with the title صَدِيق (ṣadīq) and Hebrew צֶדֶק (tzédek), which however can also be interpreted as "charitable", "giving", or "honoring".
**Possible distant relation to Akkadian 𒀭𒈪𒁲𒊑 (mīšāru, “uprightness; god personifying justice”) and Ugaritic 𐎎𐎌𐎗 (mšr, “righteousness”), cognate with Hebrew יָשָׁר (yashár, “upright, right, correct”) and يَسْر (yasr). The root ي س ر (y s r) also however denotes "to procure goods easily", "to be or grow rich", "to live in affluence or ease", "to have good fortune".
synonyms: السَعْد الأَكْبَر contrasted with Venus the lesser

maddeler.t: From مُحِيط (muḥīṭ, “ocean”), مُتَجَمِّد (mutajammid, “frozen”), active participle of تَجَمَّدَ (tajammada, “to freeze, to be frozen”), and شَمَالِيّ (šamāliyy, “northern”); literally "the northern frozen ocean."
g: Arctic Ocean (the smallest of the five oceans of the Earth, on and around the North Pole, bordered by the three continents of Asia, Europe and North America)

maddeler.e: اَللّٰهُمَّ • (allāhumma)
maddeler.t:
Extended form of الله (allāh). The origin of the ـُمَّ (-umma) is unknown. Most likely, it is a fossilized remnant of a vocative particle—akin to the very common vocative particle يا (yā)—which would have been productive in earlier Arabic. While a vocative suffix of ـُمَّ (-umma) is not attested in any other extant Arabic word, such a suffix did exist in other ancient Semitic languages such as Ugaritic and carried a vocative meaning (both the equivalents of Arabic يا (yā) and ـُمَّ (-umma) existed as ways to form the vocative in Ugaritic).
Other theories include a connection with مَا (mā), or a borrowing from Hebrew אלוהים (elohim), where the final -m is a majestic plural ending. The form is first attested in the Quran (3:26, 5:114, 8:32, 10:10, 39:46). Classical Arabic philologists in the medieval period often also struggled to determine the word’s etymology, with some, including Sibawayh, suggesting it came from a fusion of الله أُمَّـ (allāh ʔumma-), shortened from يَا أَللّٰهُ أُمَّنَا بِخَيْرٍ (yā ʔallāhu ʔummanā biḵayrin, “O God, lead us in goodness”).
s: 1948, A.D. Singer, “The Vocative in Ugaritic”, in Journal of Cuneiform Studies, page 1:
g: O God; vocative form of الله (allāh) used in invocations, oaths, etc.

g: Venice (a port city and comune, the capital of the Metropolitan City of Venice and the region of Veneto, Italy; former capital of an independent republic)

maddeler.t: Ge'ez ሐበሠት (ḥäbäśät), only attested in Aksumite inscriptions, later replaced with e.g. ብሔረ ግዕዝ (bəḥerä gəʿz), ብሔረ አግዓዝ (bəḥerä ʾägʿaz) and the Ancient Greek exonym ኢትዮጵያ (ʾityop̣ya); originally also meaning both sides of the Red Sea (which Aksum colonized). To its dominion then Old South Arabian 𐩢𐩨𐩦𐩩 (ḥbs²t) referred. In Egyptian the inhabitants of Punt were repeatedly called ḫbztyw, ḫbstyw, interpreted as from ḫbs, ḫbz, ḫbzwt (“beard”), however the moniker’s status as an actual demonym instead of just meaning literally “bearded ones” is doubtful, as well as the capability of the Egyptians to impose their term upon Aksum to be her endonym, for it to become the copiously attested Sabaean 𐩢𐩨𐩦𐩩 (ḥbs²t /⁠ḥabaśatu⁠/) and 𐩱𐩢𐩨𐩦 (ʾḥbs² /⁠ʾaḥbūśu⁠/, “Abyssinians”) too. maddeler.t:
Form IIIq (اِفْعَنْلَلَ (ifʕanlala)) of ثَعْجَرَ (ṯaʕjara, “to pour (something) out”),
from the quadriliteral root ث ع ج ر (ṯ ʕ j r); the intransitive resultant of
that transitive base, formed by infixation of ن (n) after the first
radical, analogous to Form VII (اِنْفَعَلَ (infaʕala)) among triliteral verbs.
As al-Jawharī puts it: صَبَّه فانْصَبَّ (ṣabbah fānṣabba) — "he poured it, and it poured."
g: Of tears or blood: to gush forth, to pour out in abundance.
Of clouds: to release, to discharge (rain).

In that language group the name was formed in reference to its tortuous course, on the example of Biblical Hebrew: לִוְיָה (liwyā́, “garland, wreath”) from לָוָה (lāwā́) = لَوَى (lawā, “to bend, to curve, to contort”) suffixed with ־תָּן (tān, forming agent nouns) → לִוְיָתָן (liwyāṯā́n, “leviathan, a mythological sea-serpent”). The same word up to the present Arabic form had the vowels contracted and the nisba ending added.
g: Litani (a river in Lebanon; an east-west river in South Lebanon north of Israel and south of the Zahrani)

maddeler.e: البَطَّة العَرْجَاء • (al-baṭṭa(t) al-ʕarjāʔ) f

اِشْعَانَّ • (išʕānna) XI (non-past يَشْعَانُّ (yašʕānnu), verbal noun اِشْعِينَان (išʕīnān))
maddeler.t: Form XI (اِفْعَالَّ (ifʕālla)) of the root ش ع ن (š ʕ n), built on the elative or colour-quality pattern, analogous to Form XI اِدْهَامَّ (idhāmma) from أَدْهَم (ʔadham). The root carries a base sense of dishevelment, dispersal, and bristling. Form IX اِشْعَنَّ (išʕanna) denotes the simple inchoative — hair puffing outward — while Form XI اِشْعَانَّ (išʕānna) denotes the intensive or extended state: hair not merely ruffled but fully splayed, separated, and standing on end. The verbal noun اِشْعِينَان (išʕīnān) follows the Form XI pattern اِفْعِيلَال (ifʕīlāl), the geminate lam realised as ن-ن in accordance with the root's third radical, yielding the attested form اِشْعِينَاناً (išʕīnānan) (Lisān, al-Ṣiḥāḥ, Tāj).
g: Of hair: to stand on end, to bristle and splay in all directions, to become wildly dishevelled.
Of hair: to separate, to become dispersed and dishevelled.
Of a person: to appear unkempt, with hair dusty and bristling.
dr: A man came with hair standing on end
